title: A Malayalam Action Film You've Never Heard Of Has the KGF Composer and Opens Tomorrow in Five Languages.
excerpt: Kattalan has Ravi Basrur, Antony Varghese, and the kind of ambition that used to require a Telugu megastar. The pan-India machine doesn't need permission anymore.
body:
On Wednesday, May 28, a Malayalam action thriller called Kattalan opens in theatres across India in five languages. Its director, Paul George, has no prior blockbuster credits. Its lead actor, Antony Varghese, is not a name most Hindi-speaking audiences would recognise. It was shot partly in Thailand. It has no item song, no franchise history, and no cameo from a Telugu megastar to juice the opening weekend.

It has Ravi Basrur doing the score.

If that name means nothing to you, you didn't watch KGF. Basrur composed the music for both KGF chapters — the films that turned Yash from a Kannada star into a national phenomenon and proved that a South Indian action film could outgross the entire Bollywood calendar. He also scored Salaar for Prabhas and is attached to the upcoming Toxic. When Basrur signs on to a project, it is a signal: the filmmakers believe this is the kind of film that earns its bass drops.

### What Is Kattalan?

The details are deliberately sparse. Paul George has described it as a "raw, grounded action thriller" — a phrase that in Malayalam cinema usually means less CGI, more choreography, and at least one fight sequence that will be clipped 40 million times on Instagram. Antony Varghese, who broke out with Angamaly Diaries in 2017, has built a career on exactly this kind of intense, physical performance. He isn't polished. He isn't trying to be.

B. Ajaneesh Loknath — another name from the KGF universe — is co-credited on the music. Between Basrur and Loknath, this film's soundtrack has more Kannada action cinema DNA than most Kannada films.

### The Pan-India Question

Kattalan is releasing simultaneously in Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Hindi. Two years ago, this would have been ambitious. In 2026, it's table stakes. The success of Karuppu (₹253 crore), Drishyam 3, and Raja Shivaji has established that South Indian cinema doesn't need Bollywood's permission to occupy Bollywood's screens. May 2026 has already been Bollywood's worst month in five years. Regional cinema didn't just fill the gap — it proved the gap might be permanent.

For NRIs, the shift matters more than it does domestically. The Indian diaspora's relationship with Bollywood was always emotional — it was the language of weddings, of Antakshari nights, of Sunday morning Doordarshan reruns your parents watched while you ate maggi. But the diaspora has caught up with what Indian audiences figured out years ago: the best Indian filmmaking isn't coming from Mumbai anymore. It hasn't been for a while.

### Why It Matters

Kattalan might open to ₹5 crore. It might open to ₹15 crore. The numbers, for once, are beside the point. What matters is the infrastructure: a Malayalam-language film, with a Kannada music team, shot in Thailand, releasing pan-India on the same day. Five years ago, this required a Rajamouli or a Prashanth Neel. Now it requires a first-time director with the right collaborators and a distributor willing to take the bet.

The multiplex ecosystem has changed. The subtitle infrastructure has improved. The NRI audience — particularly younger NRIs who grew up with subtitled anime, Korean drama, and Spanish-language Netflix — doesn't flinch at reading while they watch. They just want the film to be good.

### The Thursday Evening Test

If you're in the US and your local AMC or Regal is playing Kattalan with subtitles on opening night, go. If the bass from a Ravi Basrur score doesn't hit different on a proper sound system, nothing will. If the film is bad, you'll know within twenty minutes and you can switch to the Mandalorian.

But if it's good — and the talent assembled suggests it might be — you'll be telling your friends about a Malayalam action film they've never heard of. Which is, in 2026, the most Indian diaspora thing you can do.
author: Diaspora Desk
